chunks: From him, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying: 'I give a man twenty dinars for his fruit, and I say to him: When your fruit stands (matures), it is mine for that price; if I please, I take it, and if I dislike, I leave it.' He said: 'Can you not give it to him without stipulating anything?' I said: 'May I be your ransom, he does not specify anything; God knows that intention.' He said: 'It is not valid if that is his intention.'

key_terms.الثَّمَرَةُ: Fruit (specifically fruit still on the tree, awaiting harvest)
key_terms.بِالشَّيْءِ: By something (referring to an unspecified amount or quality)
key_terms.دِينَاراً: Dinar (a gold coin used as currency)
key_terms.قَامَتْ: Stands (referring to the fruit being established/mature on the tree)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying fruit with an advance payment while keeping the option to reject the harvest based on quality?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the ruling on *bay' al-thimar* (sale of unharvested fruit), emphasizing that for a conditional sale to be valid, the stipulation must be explicitly agreed upon rather than remaining a hidden internal intention (*niyya*). This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of avoiding *gharar* (uncertainty) by ensuring transparency in contractual terms, distinguishing between mere intent and binding verbal conditions.
